entries.title: Punjabi at a glance
body: Punjabi is an Indo-Aryan language of the Punjab region, split between India and Pakistan, with over 100 million speakers and large communities in Britain and Canada. In India it is written in Gurmukhi; in Pakistan it is written in Shahmukhi, a Perso-Arabic script.
The verb comes last, nouns are masculine or feminine, and postpositions follow the noun. Unusually for the region, Punjabi is tonal.

entries.title: How Gurmukhi works
body: Gurmukhi was standardized in the 16th century by Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru; the name means “from the mouth of the Guru”. Like Devanagari it is an abugida: each consonant carries a short a, and other vowels are marks around it. Three letters (ੳ, ਅ, ੲ) carry the vowels at the start of a word.
The addak ੱ doubles the next consonant, and tippi ੰ or bindi ਂ marks a nasal sound.

entries.title: Tones
entries.body: Punjabi lost the breathy sound of ਘ, ਝ, ਢ, ਧ, ਭ (gh, jh, dh, bh) and of ਹ inside a word, and gained tones in their place. At the start of a word, ਘ is said like k with a low, rising tone; after the vowel, ਹ gives a high, falling tone. The spelling stays the old one.

examples.e: whip · horse · leper: the same sounds with three tones

entries.title: “To be” and the present
entries.body: The present tense is a participle that agrees in gender and number, followed by the right form of “to be”.

entries.title: Postpositions
entries.body: These follow the noun. A masculine noun in -ā becomes -e before them: ਕਮਰਾ → ਕਮਰੇ ਵਿੱਚ.

entries.title: Numbers and Gurmukhi digits
entries.body: Gurmukhi digits are used in religious texts and sometimes on signs; everyday writing mostly uses 0–9.

entries.title: ਜੀ, the word of respect
entries.body: Adding ਜੀ (jii) after a name, a title, or even “yes” and “no” makes speech respectful: ਹਾਂਜੀ, ਨਹੀਂਜੀ, ਮਾਤਾ ਜੀ. Guests at a gurdwara cover their heads, take off their shoes, and are offered a free meal in the langar, the community kitchen.
